sources.title: Blues Harmony
sources.author: Bryn Hughes and Megan Lavengood
sources.version: Open Music Theory, Version 2, online edition; copyright 2023; accessed 2026-10-21
sources.locator: "12-Bar Blues", "Voice leading", "More Blues Schemas", and "Jazz Blues"
observations: 基本 12 小节模式分为三个四小节乐句：I；IV-I；V-IV-I-I，但各段可有 turnarounds 或局部拓展。
Blues 可由 dominant-seventh quality 的 tonic、subdominant 和 dominant 组成，并常通过 plagal motion 与大小三度并置偏离传统 tonal harmony。
16-bar blues、minor blues 与 jazz blues 是可变 schema；jazz blues 以 applied ii-V、turnaround 或 ii-V-I 改写纯 blues 动作。
和弦三音与七音可以跨五度关系平滑连接，给固定 blues frame 内的伴奏 voicing 提供局部声部逻辑。

sources.title: Swing Rhythms
sources.author: Megan Lavengood
sources.version: Open Music Theory, Version 2, online edition; copyright 2023; accessed 2026-10-21
sources.locator: "The Basic Swing Groove": "Swing eighths" and "Backbeat"; "Syncopation"
observations: Swing eighths 通常以约 2:1 的准三连音比例演奏，但实际比例取决于速度、演奏者和语境；快速度往往更接近平均。
Backbeat 是四拍中第 2、4 拍的较重音，常与 ride cymbal 上的 swing eighths 共同组成标准 swing drum beat。
第 1 拍仍是和弦变化与根音落点的重要位置，即使听觉重音转移到第 2、4 拍。
Syncopation 可由弱拍重音、休止、连线和避免 downbeat 起句产生，不能简化为单一的附点节奏。

sources.title: AABA Form and Strophic Form
sources.author: Bryn Hughes and Megan Lavengood
sources.version: Open Music Theory, Version 2, online edition; copyright 2023; accessed 2026-10-21
sources.locator: "32-Bar Song Form (AABA)"; "Sections of AABA and Strophic Forms"; "Refrains"; "Outros (O) and Codas (X)"
observations: 32-bar form is described as four eight-measure sections in the earlier Golden Age repertoire; the chapter treats this as a historical norm, not a universal rule.
The A strophe carries the principal lyric/musical material and often prolongs tonic, while B contrasts and withholds A to generate tension.
AAB bridges commonly emphasize non-tonic harmony and end on dominant harmony so that the return of A satisfies the bridge function.
A refrain is a short lyric-invariant passage inside a strophe or other section, not automatically the same structural level as a chorus or bridge.

sources.title: Transformations in Tonal Jazz: ii–V Space
sources.author: Michael McClimon
sources.locator: Introduction §§0.1–0.9; §1 ii–V space; §§2.1–2.10 tritone substitutions and Blues for Alice; §§4.1–4.3
observations: The article treats ii-V-I as a fundamental unit of tonal-jazz harmony and models compositions through constituent ii-V progressions.
The bridge of "All the Things You Are" supports multiple readings by chord tones, guide-tone lines, and local key centers; the author presents these as complementary analytical strategies.
A tritone-substituted dominant can retain dominant function while changing the bass motion from a falling fifth to a semitone, so function and root path must be assessed separately.
The ii-V space reveals harmonic patterns but does not by itself explain melody, accompaniment realization, improvisation, or the full structure of a tune.

sources.title: Guide-Tone Space: Navigating Voice-Leading Syntax in Tonal Jazz
sources.author: Sean R. Smither
sources.locator: Introduction §§0.1-0.4; §1 "Guide-Tone Theory in Jazz Pedagogy" §§1.1-1.6; §2 "Nefertiti" §§2.12-2.14; §3 §§3.1-3.3
observations: Guide tones are the chordal third and seventh; guide-tone lines connect them smoothly and are central to many jazz-pedagogy accounts of harmonic navigation.
In falling-fifth progressions, the seventh of one chord can descend by semitone to become the third of the next, while another tone is often held as a common tone.
Tritone substitution can preserve dominant function and guide-tone connections while replacing the root motion, making guide-tone coherence and tonal-center clarity separate observations.
In "Nefertiti", guide-tone continuity helps connect unusually wandering harmonies; the article uses this to show local syntax, not to prove an unchanged global tonal center.

sources.title: Beyond Strophic: Prolonged Refrains, Choruses, and Bridges in the Blues, 1923-1966
sources.author: David S. Carter
sources.locator: Introduction §§0.1–0.3; §§2.1–2.4 formal counts and 4+8 model; §§5.4–5.7 verse/bridge blend; §§6.1–6.4 solo-bridge; §§7.1–7.3 two-bridge; §§8.1–8.3 other models
observations: A corpus of 113 blues songs identifies five recurring formal approaches: 4+8, 8+8, verse/bridge blend, solo-bridge, and two-bridge.
The 4+8 model uses the last eight bars of a 12-bar blues as a prolonged refrain; the 8+8 model extends the first four bars to produce a clearer verse-chorus shape.
Vaudeville blues include AABA and ABAC examples, so strophic aab form is common but cannot define the whole genre.

In some verse/bridge blends, the twelve-bar harmonic pattern remains while stop time, melody, texture, and solos create contrast; the article relates such hybridity to Black migration, urban commercial audiences, and interacting musical/social conditions.

sources.title: A Platonic Model of Funky Rhythms
sources.author: Richard Cohn
sources.locator: Introduction §§0.1–0.4; §§1.1–1.10 Ellington doo-wah analysis; §§2.8–2.11 Platonic model; §§3.1–3.4 generative framing
observations: Big-band jazz and several African-diasporic popular repertoires project duple meter across quarter pulses, half-note beats, four-bar phrases, eight-bar phrase pairs, and 32-bar AABA quatrains while overlaying recurring three-unit spans.
In "It Don't Mean a Thing", the bass and hocketing chords support a fast duple frame while two- and three-unit relations animate the groove.
The brass short-long response patterns are analyzed as cyclical doo-wahs; accent and timbre participate in the rhythmic structure rather than merely decorating it.
The strong duple-AABA model is tied to a specific big-band and popular-music repertoire, so it should not be promoted to a rule for every jazz style.

sources.title: The Power of Anacrusis: Engendered Feeling in Groove-Based Musics
sources.author: Matthew W. Butterfield
sources.locator: Introduction §§1–4; §§10–22 anacrusis and rhythmic layers; §§32–37 swing groove and backbeat timing; §§40–52 Chameleon measurements and groove return
observations: Groove is modeled as an interaction between a recurring syntactical rhythm and expressive microrhythmic discrepancies; participatory differences under roughly 50 ms may create qualitative push, relaxation, or lay-back effects.
In the conventional swing groove, the ride pattern, swing-eighth structure, and walking-bass relation provide a framework against which backbeat timing is heard.
An on-top hi-hat backbeat can intensify forward drive, while a late 'in-the-pocket' backbeat can relax the feel without removing swing.
Listeners learn tempo-metrical and microtiming norms, helping explain why subtle timing differences can distinguish the feels of different Swing Era big bands.

sources.title: Referents in the Palimpsests of Jazz: Disentangling Theme from Improvisation in Recordings of Standard Jazz Tunes
sources.author: Sean R. Smither
sources.locator: §1 "The Problematics of Analyzing Standard Jazz Tunes" §§1.1-1.12; §2 "Representing Referents" §§2.1-2.5; §3 "Referent Defaults" §§3.1-3.3
observations: Jazz tunes are flexible, continually reinterpreted structures rather than fixed works with one definitive recording or lead sheet.
A provisionally constructed referent uses multiple versions to separate tune-based material from improvisational departures; harmonic defaults may be weighted or equally viable alternatives.
Head-solos-head is identified as a common modern-jazz frame: the head establishes the tune, solos explore transformations, and the head returns.
Written big-band arrangements are characterized by comparatively thick harmonizations, counterlines, horn textures, soli, and ensemble hits; small-group arrangements may predetermine far less.

sources.title: Form and Voice Leading in Early Beatles Songs
sources.author: Drew F. Nobile
sources.locator: Introduction §0.1; §1 "SRDC-B form" §§1.1-1.3; §2 voice-leading model §§2.1 onward; §5 off-tonic beginnings
observations: The early-Beatles AABA model calls each A section a verse and each B section a bridge or middle eight; full-song repetitions can yield AABABA or AABAABA.
Within A, SRDC means statement, restatement, departure, and conclusion; the conclusion often carries the refrain or title lyric.
In the general model, S and R prolong tonic, D begins on IV or another pre-dominant, C completes the cadence, and B starts off-tonic before a dominant retransition.
Bridges tend to contrast both harmony and melody and prepare the return of A; songs still engage the model through deviations rather than fitting it mechanically.

sources.title: Sentential Lyric-Types in the Great American Songbook
sources.author: Michael R. Callahan
sources.locator: Introduction §§1.1-1.4; classification method and Sentential Lyric-Types through §6; full-song interaction examples in §8
observations: Tin Pan Alley and musical-theatre songs commonly use regular eight- and sixteen-measure phrases, with AABA or ABAC combining two or four phrases into a song.
A musical sentence begins with two basic ideas, continues by building momentum or increasing fragmentation, and reaches a half or authentic cadence.

Lyrics can reproduce the same presentation-continuation-cadence logic through repetition, rhyme, line length, acceleration, and semantic shifts; words and music may cooperate, compensate, or contradict each other.
The interaction between regular frameworks and local irregularity supports using AABA/ABAC as an analytical expectation rather than a template for every work.

supports: Ross's analysis of the finale as a hybrid sonata-rondo/sonata-form movement, while documenting the contested formal labeling; 2/4 meter and dance character.

The alternative is shorter and lighter than the multi-section Grosse Fuge in Ross's characterization, but the new finale still contains 493 measures; its development section is 61 measures. These data do not establish an objectively optimal whole-cycle duration or balance.
Ross's specific account of thematic economy, revised momentum in the development, false and tonic recapitulations, voice placement, and thematic reuse in the coda.
Ross's source-based account of revisions in composing score Autograph 19c and fair copy Grasnick 10, subject to her stated uncertainty about exact revision chronology.
sources.does_not_support: A definitive performance choice between the two finales; authorial motive reducible to commercial/popular pressure; a single uncontested formal label; independent verification of Ross's transcription or chronology; a universal recipe for finale writing.
